content.title: Comma After Introductory Element
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the correct use of commas to separate introductory elements—such as dependent clauses, participial phrases, and long prepositional phrases—from the main independent clause of a sentence.
learning_objectives: Identify introductory elements at the start of a sentence.
Apply the rule for placing a comma after introductory chunks.
Distinguish between introductory phrases and sentence subjects.
Recognize when a comma is optional for short introductory phrases.

sections.title: Defining Introductory Elements
sections.content: An introductory element is a word, phrase, or clause that appears at the beginning of a sentence before the main subject and verb. These elements provide context, such as time, place, or condition, but cannot stand alone as complete sentences. Common types include: 1) Dependent clauses (starting with words like 'Although', 'Because', or 'If'), 2) Participial phrases (starting with -ing or -ed verbs), and 3) Prepositional phrases (starting with words like 'In', 'After', or 'During').

sections.title: The General Rule
sections.content: Place a single comma immediately after the introductory element to separate it from the independent main clause. This comma signals a brief pause and helps the reader identify where the main subject of the sentence begins. If the introductory element is a dependent clause, the comma is mandatory. If it is a long prepositional phrase (usually four words or more), the comma is highly recommended for clarity.

sections.title: Exceptions and Short Openings
sections.content: If the opening chunk is very short (typically one or two words), the comma is often optional unless it is needed to prevent misreading. However, never place a comma after an opening chunk if that chunk is actually the subject of the sentence. For example, in the sentence 'Running is my favorite hobby,' 'Running' is the subject, so no comma should follow it.

worked_examples.question: Choose the best punctuation for the following sentence: 'After finishing the steep climb the hikers reached the ridge.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the opening chunk: 'After finishing the steep climb' is a participial phrase functioning as an introductory element. 2. Apply the rule: Place one comma after the introductory phrase to separate it from the main clause. 3. Result: 'After finishing the steep climb, the hikers reached the ridge.' 4. Final check: Reading aloud reveals a natural pause after 'climb,' and the main subject 'the hikers' follows immediately.

worked_examples.question: Identify if a comma is needed: 'Because the weather was clear we decided to go camping.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify the opening chunk: 'Because the weather was clear' is a dependent clause. 2. Apply the rule: Dependent clauses at the start of a sentence must be followed by a comma. 3. Result: 'Because the weather was clear, we decided to go camping.'

common_mistakes: Omitting the comma after a long introductory phrase, which creates a 'run-on' feel and reduces clarity.
Placing a comma after the subject of the sentence (e.g., 'The tall man, walked home' is incorrect).
Using a semicolon instead of a comma to set off an introductory phrase.
Placing the comma too early in the phrase (e.g., 'After, finishing the climb...').
exam_tips: If you see a sentence starting with 'If', 'Because', 'Although', or 'When', look for a comma before the main subject.
Use the 'Read Aloud' test: if you naturally pause before the subject, a comma is likely required.
Check the word count: if a prepositional phrase is four words or longer, it almost always needs a comma on the ACT.
Verify the subject: ensure the word following the comma is the actual subject performing the action.
content.recap: Introductory elements set the stage for the main clause. Use a comma after dependent clauses, participial phrases, and long prepositional phrases to separate them from the main subject. Do not use a comma if the opening word is the subject of the sentence.

knowledge_claims.content: An introductory element is a phrase or clause that appears before the main subject and verb to provide context.
A single comma should be placed immediately after an introductory element to separate it from the independent main clause.
Introductory elements often take the form of dependent clauses, participial phrases, or prepositional phrases.
A comma is mandatory when a sentence begins with a dependent clause starting with conjunctions like 'Because' or 'Although'.
To verify comma placement, identify the main subject and ensure the comma is placed directly before it and after the introductory chunk.
It is a mistake to place a comma after an opening word or phrase if that element functions as the subject of the sentence.
The comma after an introductory element signals a brief pause for the reader, enhancing sentence clarity.
For very short introductory phrases of one or two words, the comma is often optional unless needed for clarity.
Unlike independent clauses joined by a semicolon, an introductory element cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.
A prepositional phrase of four words or more at the start of a sentence typically requires a comma.
Participial phrases at the start of a sentence, often ending in -ing or -ed, function as introductory elements requiring a comma.
Placing a comma in the middle of an introductory phrase rather than at the end is a common punctuation error.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

For the wording marked [1], which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

options.A: After three months of fundraising, a neighborhood restoration crew began
options.B: After three months of fundraising a neighborhood restoration crew began
options.C: After three months of fundraising; a neighborhood restoration crew began
options.D: After three months of fundraising: a neighborhood restoration crew began

items.explanation: A comma correctly separates the introductory phrase from the independent clause.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

For the wording marked [1], which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

options.A: After several cloudy evenings a coastal ecology class began
options.B: After several cloudy evenings; a coastal ecology class began
options.C: After several cloudy evenings, a coastal ecology class began
options.D: After several cloudy evenings: a coastal ecology class began

items.explanation: A comma correctly separates the introductory phrase from the independent clause.

videoLesson.title: Place Comma After Introductory Element
videoLesson.description: Recognize introductory chunks—dependent clauses, participial phrases, or long prepositional phrases. Place one comma after them; omit it for very short openings or when they act as the subject.
